etymologies.text: 取(と)る (toru, “to take”) + 出(だ)す (dasu, “to put out”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 地 (dijᴴ). The goon reading, so likely the initial borrowing. Compare modern Mandarin dì.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 地 (dijᴴ). The kan'on reading, so likely a later borrowing. The devoicing of the initial consonant might indicate a dialectal source. Compare modern Hakka thi, Min Nan tī.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/tabi₁/ → /tabi/
From Old Japanese. Appears in the Man'yōshū, completed no earlier than 759 and one of the oldest extant texts in the Japanese language.
May be cognate with 度 (tabi, “the time when something happens”); both terms have the same pitch accent, the same ancient vowel values, and some semantic overlap.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 旅 (MC ljoX, “a military unit of 500 men; to go [on a sortie; on a trip or journey]”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. First cited to the Kojiki of 712.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 根 (MC kon). First cited in Japanese contexts in the 法華義疏 (Hokke Gisho) dated to 615, a commentary on the Buddhist Lotus Sutra that was written in Classical Chinese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Cognate with 止(と)める (tomeru, “to stop”) and 停(と)める (tomeru, “to park (a car)”), and their mediopassive counterpart 止(と)まる (tomaru, “to stop”). Likely also related to 留(とど)める (todomeru, “to keep”) above, and to its mediopassive counterpart 止(とど)まる (todomaru, “to remain”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 盆 (MC bwon). Compare modern Mandarin 盆 (pén).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Short for 盂蘭盆 (Urabon) or 盂蘭盆会 (Urabon'e), from Middle Chinese 盂蘭盆 (hju lan bwon) or 盂蘭盆會 (hju lan bwon hwajᴴ) (compare modern Mandarin 盂蘭盆 /盂兰盆 (yúlánpén) or 盂蘭盆會／盂兰盆会 (yúlánpénhuì)), a transcription of Pali ullumpana (“raising, helping”), present participle of Pali verb ullumpati (“to raise up, to help”).
A number of Japanese dictionaries state that this term derives from Sanskrit उल्लम्बन (ullambana), purportedly meaning “hanging upside-down” in reference to the souls of the dead being tortured in hell by being strung up by their feet.
However, this meaning doesn't match the semantics very well, given that the urabon ceremonies are about helping the dead, closer in meaning to the “helping” sense of the Pali verb. This suggests that explanations of the dead hanging upside-down in hell are more likely to be folk etymologies based on a mistaken connection to the Sanskrit verb, rather than a more direct semantic link to the Pali. Alternatively, Junjirō Takakusu (apud Ashikaga, 1951) propounded that the origin was in fact Pali ullumbana, a colloquial corruption of Pali ullumpana (“raising up; saving; helping”), and that the etymology was mistakenly attributed to Sanskrit.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Alteration from bon, where the final moraic n changed to ni. Compare the Japanese given name 紫苑 with similar development of reading Shioni from Shion.
Obsolete reading.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 羨(うらや)む (urayamu, “to envy, to be jealous of”, mizenkei form 羨(うらや)ま (urayama)) + しい (-shii, adjectivizing suffix evoking quality of the suffixed term).羨(うらや)む (urayamu) is from 心(うら) (ura, “heart, inner feelings”) + 病(や)む (yamu, “affected, afflicted, worried”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, first attested in the Nihon Shoki (720 CE).
The iku part is possibly derived from either 射くう (ikuu, “to shoot (an arrow)”, obsolete), 的 (ikuha, “target”, archaic), or classical verb 生く (iku, “to exist, live; bring to life”). The iku- in the first and second etyma appear to be cognate.
The final sa is likely from 矢 (sa, “arrow”, obsolete) or さ (-sa, suffix attached to verbs to refer to the time that the activity is done, or to nouns indicating direction).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Shift from verb 通(つう)ずる (tsūzuru), by natural progression from サ行変格活用 (sa-gyō henkaku katsuyō, “s-irregular conjugation”) verbs ending in -uru to 上一段活用 (kami ichidan katsuyō, “upper monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -iru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese.
Thought to be derived from 隠(おん) (on, “to hide; hidden from sight”).
